attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithfully captures the denial. Leaving out the separate clause about committing to outcomes is reasonable.

contract.note: Under the contract, one successful task contradicts the claim. But 'powerful tool for handling complex tasks' ordinarily means dependable capability across tasks, not one success in eight. The contract itself flags this distinction, then sets it aside against the speaker.

evidence.note: Independent test 8 shows a detailed, accurate building-code analysis, which undercuts 'by any extension'. Yet the same reviewer judged the agent unreliable and generally poor, with 1 near-perfect result in 8.
Independent test: a fairly simple reservation task worked but was slow and needed human help. This does not settle whether the agent is powerful on complex tasks.

reviews.rationale: The categorical 'by any extension' is undercut by one documented strong result on a substantial task (e1). The broader point holds: the same independent tester found the agent generally unreliable and poor, and e2 shows slow, assisted completion of a simple task. Small case studies cannot settle representative capability either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'maybe' as a hedge on the revenue figure and keeps the no-profit part firm. The companies, period and accounting basis are unspecified in the source.

contract.note: The contract says plainly that the missing company list, period and accounting basis prevent a matched calculation. The Q2 2025 frame is used only as an observation window, not as the claim's measure. That is fair, though the frame is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: OpenAI's annualized run rate for one company, with exclusions. It is not realized revenue for the group, and the company figure is confirmed by OpenAI itself.
Secondary report: OpenAI's first-half 2025 revenue of $4.3B against $6.7B in R&D. This points to a loss at one company but is not a group-wide figure for revenue or bottom-line profit.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched total of realized revenue or bottom-line profit for the unspecified group of AI companies. The OpenAI-only figures (run rate, first-half revenue and R&D) are different measures and scopes, so they cannot confirm or refute 'maybe $40B revenue, no profit'.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: This compound sentence mixes present observations, an unqualified 'not going to' forecast and a causal reason. Scoring the firm forecast with no deadline is appropriate. The remark about boosters' motives is rightly excluded.

contract.note: The contract counts a documented replacement of a job or staffing need as contradiction and does not treat continued non-replacement as support. That is consistent with an open-ended 'will not'. The tie of autonomy to doing an entire job comes from the speaker's own context.

evidence.note: Anthropic's account of itself: a team handed work to agents and was reassigned. It does not show how much supervision was needed, whether whole roles were covered, or any independent corroboration, so it falls short of the contradiction standard.
METR's measurement of bounded tasks and its uncertainty. It does not measure job replacement.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, so it can only be resolved by a qualifying deployment. The strongest item is a company disclosure about reassigning a team. It lacks detail on supervision and full role coverage, and has no independent corroboration, so it does not meet the early-resolution rule. Absence of replacement cannot support the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: In context, Zitron grants that the model produced the outputs but says researchers executed them and gave prompts. The normalised claim about autonomous execution matches that. His speculation about why prompts were withheld is hedged and rightly not scored.

contract.note: Reading the claim as denying autonomous execution matches the speaker's own bracketed remarks (the researcher copy-pasted model outputs). The broader reading, that the model made no choices, is flagged but not the one used.

evidence.note: The original ARC transcript documents the hiring task given to the model, a researcher operating the browser, and a researcher replacing the model's reasoning with a hint.
The contemporaneous ARC account confirms the hint, but credits the model with generating the commands, choices and messages. That limits any broader reading of 'any of these actions'.

reviews.rationale: The original records show the model was given the task, a researcher executed the browser actions, and a researcher intervened by substituting reasoning. So this was not an unattended autonomous transaction, which meets the support condition. The model did generate the decisions and messages, so the claim holds only on the execution reading.
